title: Chapter 2 — Of Individualism In Democratic Countries
paragraphs: I have shown how, in ages of equality, every man looks for his opinions within himself. I am now going to show how, in those same ages, all his feelings are turned toward himself alone. Individualism *a is a new word, born of a new idea. Our forefathers knew only egotism. Egotism is a passionate and exaggerated love of self, which leads a man to relate everything to his own person and to prefer himself to everything in the world. Individualism is a calm and considered feeling that disposes each member of the community to cut himself off from the mass of his fellow creatures and to withdraw with his family and his friends. Once he has formed a little circle of his own in this way, he is willing to leave society at large to itself. Egotism comes from blind instinct. Individualism comes more from mistaken judgment than from corrupt feelings. It arises as much from deficiencies of the mind as from the perversity of the heart. Egotism blights the seed of every virtue. Individualism at first undermines only the virtues of public life, but in the long run it attacks and destroys all the others, and in the end it is absorbed into plain egotism. Egotism is a vice as old as the world, and it belongs to no one form of society more than another. Individualism is of democratic origin, and it threatens to spread in the same proportion as the equality of conditions.

[Footnote a: [I adopt the expression of the original, however strange it may seem to English ears, partly because it illustrates the remark on the introduction of general terms into democratic language that was made in an earlier chapter, and partly because I know of no English word that corresponds to it exactly. The chapter itself defines the meaning the author gives it. — Translator’s Note.]]

Among aristocratic nations, families stay in the same condition for centuries, often on the same spot, so that all generations become, as it were, contemporaries. A man almost always knows his forefathers and respects them. He thinks he can already see his remote descendants, and he loves them. He willingly takes on duties toward both, and he will often sacrifice his personal gratifications for those who went before him and those who will come after him. Aristocratic institutions also have the effect of binding every man closely to several of his fellow citizens. The classes of an aristocratic people are sharply marked and permanent, so each of them is regarded by its own members as a kind of lesser country, more tangible and more cherished than the country at large. In aristocratic communities all citizens occupy fixed positions, one above another. As a result, each of them always sees above him a man whose patronage he needs, and below him another man whose cooperation he may claim. Men living in aristocratic ages are therefore almost always closely attached to something outside their own sphere, and they are often ready to forget themselves. It is true that in those ages the idea of human fellowship is faint, and men seldom think of sacrificing themselves for mankind. But they often sacrifice themselves for other men. In democratic ages, by contrast, each individual’s duties to the human race are much clearer, but devoted service to any one man becomes rarer. The bond of human affection is extended, but it is loosened.

Among democratic nations new families are constantly springing up, others are constantly falling away, and all that remain change their condition. The thread of time is broken at every moment, and the track of the generations is wiped out. Those who went before are soon forgotten, and no one has any idea of those who will come after. A man’s interest is confined to those closest to himself. As each class draws nearer to the other classes and mixes with them, its members become indifferent to one another and like strangers. Aristocracy had made a chain of all the members of the community, from the peasant to the king. Democracy breaks that chain and severs every link of it. As social conditions become more equal, the number grows of people who are neither rich enough nor powerful enough to have any great influence over their fellow creatures, but who have nevertheless acquired or kept enough education and fortune to satisfy their own wants. They owe nothing to any man, and they expect nothing from any man. They form the habit of always considering themselves as standing alone, and they tend to imagine that their whole destiny is in their own hands. Thus democracy not only makes every man forget his ancestors, but also hides his descendants from him and separates him from his contemporaries. It throws him back forever upon himself alone, and threatens in the end to confine him entirely within the solitude of his own heart.
